cards.title: A plan-review button appears in the pane header while Claude waits for plan approval
cards.user_does: Lets Claude finish planning in plan mode, then looks at that pane's header.
cards.user_sees: A small "Review plan" icon button in the pane header for as long as Claude is waiting on its exit-plan approval; clicking it opens the review sheet.
rules: The button shows only when the pane's live status carries a plan-approval prompt that includes plan text.
Other approvals (for example a shell-command approval) never show the button.
A pane with no pending prompt, or a host too old to report the plan, shows nothing.
The plan-approval wait itself comes from the agent status hooks (the plan-approval tool event maps to the waiting state).
Claude sends both a pre-tool event and a permission-request event for its plan-exit step, each carrying the full plan text; either one is enough to show the button.
acceptance: Claude asks to leave plan mode → the header shows the review button; approve in the terminal → the button disappears.
Claude asks to run a shell command → no review button appears.
cards.compat: Claude Code fires PreToolUse and PermissionRequest for ExitPlanMode; each carries the plan in tool_input.plan.

cards.title: Plan review sheet splits the plan into sections the user can comment on
cards.user_does: Opens the review sheet, reads the plan, and adds a comment under any section or a general note at the bottom.
cards.user_sees: A sheet sliding in from the right edge, titled for plan review, with the plan rendered as formatted markdown in blocks; each block has its own comment control, comments can be removed, and a free-text general note field sits below.
rules: Sections break at blank lines; blank lines inside a fenced code block do not break a section.
Runs of blank lines (leading, trailing or repeated) never produce empty sections.
Each section knows its 1-based start and end line, used to label comments.
An empty or all-blank plan yields no sections.
acceptance: A plan of three paragraphs with a fenced block containing a blank line → three sections, the fenced block intact in one.
Add a comment to section 2 → it appears under that section and can be deleted.

cards.title: Approve from the sheet lets Claude go ahead with the plan
cards.user_does: Clicks "Approve" in the review sheet.
cards.user_sees: The sheet closes and Claude proceeds exactly as if the user had picked the allow option in the terminal prompt; any draft comments for that plan are discarded.
rules: Approve is always enabled while the plan is still waiting, with or without comments.
Approving answers the terminal prompt with its first (allow) choice.
Approving clears the stored draft for that pane and plan.
In most Claude versions that first choice also accepts later file edits automatically; the button keeps the neutral label Approve.
acceptance: Open the sheet, click Approve → Claude leaves plan mode and starts work; reopening shows no review button.

cards.title: Request changes sends the plan back to Claude with the user's comments
cards.user_does: Adds one or more section comments or a general note, then clicks "Request changes".
cards.user_sees: The button shows how many comments are pending; on click the sheet closes, Claude's plan prompt is dismissed, and a chat message arrives in the pane asking Claude to revise and re-present the plan, listing each comment with its line range and a short excerpt, then the general note.
rules: The button is disabled until there is at least one comment or a non-blank note.
Kolux first dismisses the plan prompt, then waits for the pane to leave the plan-approval state before sending the feedback.
If the state never changes, the feedback is sent anyway after a ceiling of about 3 seconds; if the pane already left the prompt, it is sent at once.
A pending send can be cancelled before or after it fires.
Feedback order: a fixed request-to-revise header, then each comment (line label, excerpt, comment text), then the trimmed general note.
Sending clears the stored draft.
acceptance: With no comments and no note → Request changes is disabled.
Add two comments and click Request changes → Claude receives one message naming both line ranges and revises its plan.
Simulate a pane whose status never updates → the feedback still arrives after about 3 seconds.

cards.title: Unsent review comments survive closing and reopening the sheet
cards.user_does: Writes comments, closes the sheet without sending, and opens it again later.
cards.user_sees: The same comments and note are still there; a new plan from Claude starts with an empty draft.
rules: Drafts are held in memory per pane and per exact plan text; a revised plan is a different draft.
Drafts do not survive an app restart.
At most 128 drafts are kept; the oldest is dropped first.
acceptance: Comment, close, reopen → comment still present.
Claude presents a revised plan → the sheet opens with no comments.

cards.title: Very long plans are shortened in the sheet with a notice pointing to the terminal
cards.user_does: Opens the review sheet for a very long plan.
cards.user_sees: The sheet shows as much of the plan as fits, with a notice that it was shortened and the full text is in the terminal.
rules: The status payload carrying the plan has a size ceiling of 16,000 characters; the plan is cut to the longest length that fits.
The prompt's short summary is always kept; if even an empty plan cannot fit, the plan is dropped and the review button does not show.
The shortened notice appears only when the plan was actually cut.
acceptance: A 40,000-character plan → sheet opens with the shortened notice; a short plan → no notice.

cards.title: The sheet goes read-only once Claude is no longer waiting on that plan
cards.user_does: Keeps the sheet open while the plan prompt is answered in the terminal, or Claude moves on.
cards.user_sees: A notice that Claude is no longer waiting on this plan, and both action buttons disabled.
rules: The sheet compares its plan with the pane's current live plan; any mismatch or absence disables Approve and Request changes.
acceptance: Open the sheet, then approve in the terminal → the sheet shows the notice and its buttons are disabled.

cards.title: Plan review opened from the native-chat approval card
cards.user_does: In the native chat view, clicks the plan-review action on an approval card.
cards.user_sees: The same review sheet, sharing drafts with the pane-header entry point.
rules: Second entry point only; native chat is flagged off by default.
acceptance: n/a — decision item

cards.title: Protected actions: Claude pauses for a yes/no before a dangerous shell command
cards.user_does: Lets a Claude Code session run in a Kolux pane; Claude tries a command that matches a protected rule.
cards.user_sees: Claude stops before running it and shows its own permission prompt with a reason naming the Kolux rule (for example a force-push to main), saying nothing runs until allowed and a denial keeps it blocked; the pane shows the waiting state. Allow once runs it; deny leaves it unrun.
rules: Covers Claude Code only, through its pre-tool hook; Codex and other agents are not guarded, and Settings says so.
Only Claude's Bash and PowerShell tools are checked; other tools pass through.
Requires the agent status hooks to be on (they are on by default).
No match, a non-shell tool, a non-pre-tool event, or an unreadable hook body all get a neutral reply so Claude's normal permission flow continues (fail open, never block).
The rule label in the reason is capped at 120 characters.
The workspace for path rules is the pane's worktree folder, not just the current directory; the project id selects per-project rules.
Switching a rule off stops it asking on the very next command, with no restart.
OpenClaude runs through the same managed Claude hook, so it is guarded too; Codex is not, because its hooks can only deny, never ask.
acceptance: Claude runs a force-push of main → Claude's permission prompt appears with the Kolux reason; choose deny → nothing is pushed.
Claude runs a plain status command → no prompt.
Turn the matching rule off and repeat → the command runs without a prompt.
Send the hook a malformed body → neutral reply, Claude continues.
cards.compat: Claude Code PreToolUse hook: reply is either an empty JSON object (no decision) or hookSpecificOutput with hookEventName PreToolUse, permissionDecision ask and a permissionDecisionReason; checks tool_name Bash or PowerShell and tool_input.command; accepts form and raw-JSON hook bodies.

cards.title: Default rules guard git history: force-push to main and throwing away uncommitted work
cards.user_does: Has Claude run git commands in a worktree.
cards.user_sees: A pause before a force-push or delete aimed at main or master, and before a hard reset or forced clean; ordinary pushes, feature-branch force-pushes, soft resets and dry-run cleans run untouched.
rules: Force means a force flag (including lease and mirror forms, and combined short flags) or a plus-prefixed refspec; delete means a delete flag or an empty-source refspec onto main.
Asks when the destination is main or master, the current branch (HEAD or the at-sign shorthand), a shell substitution, or when no refspec is given, or with push-all or mirror.
Git global options before the subcommand (change directory, config, git-dir) are skipped.
Discard rule: a hard reset, or a clean with the force flag; a reset without hard and a dry-run clean do not ask.
acceptance: git push --force origin main → asks; git push -f → asks; git push origin :main → asks.
git push -f origin @:main and git push --force origin @ → ask.
git push --force origin feature/login → runs; git push origin main → runs; git push origin @ → runs.
git reset --hard → asks; git clean -fdx → asks; git reset --soft HEAD~1 and git clean -n → run.

cards.title: Default rule: pause before dropping or truncating database objects
cards.user_does: Has Claude run a database client with destructive SQL.
cards.user_sees: A pause before a drop or truncate sent through a database client, or before a whole-database drop tool; mentions of the same words in commit messages or searches do not ask.
rules: Only database clients count (Postgres, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, Mongo shells, and hosted-DB CLIs such as Supabase, Prisma, Wrangler, BigQuery, DuckDB and similar).
Destructive means DROP of a table, database, schema, view, index, user or role, or TRUNCATE.
The whole command line is checked, so SQL piped or fed by heredoc into the client is seen.
The dedicated drop-database tool always asks.
acceptance: psql with -c "DROP TABLE users;" → asks; echo "truncate table orders" | psql prod → asks; dropdb production → asks.
git commit -m "drop table users" → runs; grep -rn "DROP TABLE" migrations/ → runs.

cards.title: Default rules guard live services: Stripe live changes, infrastructure apply, production deploys
cards.user_does: Has Claude run payment, infrastructure or deploy CLIs.
cards.user_sees: A pause before changing live Stripe data, before applying or destroying infrastructure, and before deploying to production; read-only and preview commands run untouched.
rules: Stripe: any live secret or restricted key in the command asks, unless the command is a text search; otherwise the Stripe CLI asks with its live flag or a mutating verb (create, update, delete, cancel, refund, post and similar) in its first few words; listening and listing do not ask.
Infrastructure: Terraform/OpenTofu apply or destroy, Terragrunt apply/destroy (including run-all), Pulumi up/update/destroy, CDK deploy/destroy; plan and init do not ask.

Production deploy: a production flag (prod, production, env=prod, -e production) together with a deploy CLI (Vercel, Netlify, Firebase, Wrangler, Fly, Railway, Heroku, gcloud, az and similar) or a deploy verb; a deploy with no production flag and package installs with a production flag do not ask.
The rules are deliberately narrow so the user is not trained to click allow by reflex.
acceptance: stripe subscriptions cancel sub_test → asks; stripe listen and stripe customers list → run; grep -rn "sk_live_" src/ → runs.
terraform apply -auto-approve → asks; npx cdk deploy → asks; terraform plan → runs.
vercel --prod → asks; npx wrangler deploy --env production → asks; vercel deploy → runs; npm install --production → runs.

cards.title: Default rule: pause before recursively deleting a folder outside the workspace
cards.user_does: Has Claude run a recursive delete in Bash, cmd or PowerShell.
cards.user_sees: A pause when the target is outside the worktree, is the worktree itself or its git folder, or cannot be known; deleting build output inside the worktree or scratch folders in temp runs untouched.
rules: Recursive deletes: rm with a recursive flag; rd, rmdir, del and erase with the subtree switch (also when switches are joined); PowerShell Remove-Item and its aliases with a recurse flag or any abbreviation of it, reading path and literal-path values.

Asks when the target is outside the workspace, equals the workspace, is its git folder, is unknowable (a variable, another user's home, a drive-relative path) or is missing because the names come from a pipe.
Temp folders never ask (TMPDIR, TEMP, /tmp, /var/tmp) unless the path climbs out with ..; globs are judged by their folder.
cd, pushd and Set-Location earlier in the same command move the base for relative paths; bare cd goes home; popd, bare pushd and cd to a variable make the base unknown.
With no known workspace, the starting directory stands in for it; with neither known, relative recursive deletes ask.
Paths are compared lexically only, never touching the disk; Git Bash drive paths fold to Windows form; Windows comparisons ignore case.
acceptance: rm -rf / , rm -rf ~/Documents, rm -rf .., rm -rf ., rm -rf .git, rm -rf $BUILD_DIR → each asks.
cd $HOME && rm -rf build → asks; cd && rm -rf build → asks; popd && rm -rf build → asks; find . | xargs rm -rf → asks.
Remove-Item -Recurse -Force on the user's home folder → asks; Get-ChildItem | Remove-Item -Recurse → asks; rd /s /q on the Documents folder → asks.
rm -rf node_modules dist .next, rm -rf ./dist/*, cd packages/web && rm -rf node_modules, rm -rf /tmp/kolux-test-123, rd /s /q node_modules → each runs.

cards.title: Protected commands are caught even when wrapped, chained, nested or encoded (audit bypass checks)
cards.user_does: Has Claude run a dangerous command hidden inside a wrapper, a chain or another shell.
cards.user_sees: The same pause as for the bare command, naming the segment that matched; harmless commands in the same shapes still run.
rules: Every program in a chain is checked (semicolon, ampersand, pipe, and/or operators, newlines, grouping), plus command substitutions and backticks, nested up to four levels.

Wrapper programs are looked through (sudo, doas, nohup, time, nice, env, xargs, timeout, npx, bunx, exec, start and similar, plus package-runner subcommands and leading VAR=value assignments); their value-taking options never count as the command, and the timeout duration is skipped.

Inner commands are read from POSIX shells with -c, cmd with /c or /k (including the doubled-slash Git Bash form), PowerShell with -Command or a base64 encoded command (any unambiguous abbreviation), eval/iex, and wsl exec forms.

PowerShell options that take a value (execution policy, window style, working directory, input/output format and similar, including short aliases) skip their value; a -File invocation has no inner command.

These close the 2026-10-04 audit bypasses S1 (PowerShell value flags), S2 (wrapper option values), S3 (joined cmd switches and doubled slash), S4 (bare cd/popd) and the at-sign-as-HEAD gap; the rebuild must pass them from day one.
A command merely echoed as text does not ask.
acceptance: bash -c "rm -rf /" → asks; echo $(rm -rf /) → asks; cmd /c "rd /s /q C:\Users" → asks.
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command "terraform apply -auto-approve" → asks; same with -ep bypass, -WindowStyle Hidden, -of text, or as an encoded command → asks.
powershell -File x.ps1 ; terraform apply -auto-approve → asks.
cmd //c "rd /s /q C:\Windows" → asks; rd /s/q C:\Windows → asks; del /q/s C:\Windows\x → asks.
sudo -u root rm -rf /var/lib/app, nice -n 10 …, env -u FOO …, timeout 5 …, sudo -uroot … → each asks; timeout 30s terraform apply -auto-approve → asks.
sudo -u root ls build, timeout 5 ls, nice -n 10 echo hi, powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command "echo hi", rd /s/q build, echo "rm -rf /" → each runs.

cards.title: Protected actions settings section on the Safety page
cards.user_does: Opens Settings → Safety → Protected actions.
cards.user_sees: A short explanation, a plain note that only Claude Code is covered, a note that status hooks must be on, a master switch "Ask before protected actions", and one row per rule with its name, examples and an on/off toggle.
rules: The master switch off means no rule ever asks; on is the default.

The seven built-in rules are listed by plain name: Stripe changes, force-push to main, deleting database tables, infrastructure changes, production deploys, deleting folders outside the workspace, throwing away uncommitted work.
Turning a built-in off records it as disabled; it can be turned back on any time.
The section is reachable from settings search.
In the rebuild this section lives on the kept Safety page.
acceptance: Toggle the force-push rule off → a following force-push of main runs without a prompt; toggle on → it asks again.
Switch the master toggle off → no protected command asks.
cards.compat: Settings data the importer must carry: protected-actions block with enabled flag, list of disabled built-in rule ids, custom rules, and per-project overrides.

cards.title: Users add their own protected rules by prefix, text or regular expression
cards.user_does: In the Protected actions section, enters an optional label, picks a match type (starts with command, contains text, or regular expression), types a pattern such as npm publish, and clicks "Add rule".
cards.user_sees: The new rule in the list with its match-type badge and pattern, a toggle and a delete button; an invalid pattern shows a plain-language error and nothing is saved.
rules: Starts-with compares the program and its leading words, ignoring case; contains compares whitespace-collapsed lowercase text; regex is case-insensitive.
Validation rejects an empty pattern, a pattern over 500 characters, an invalid regex, a repeated group that already repeats, and three or more back-to-back overlapping unbounded repeats.
Neighbouring repeats of disjoint character sets (whitespace then non-whitespace, letters then digits) stay allowed, as do ordinary regexes with up to two adjacent repeats.
A risky regex that reaches the settings file by hand is never run; regex input is capped at 4,096 characters (audit S6).
A missing label falls back to the pattern.
acceptance: Add a contains rule for npm publish → Claude running npm publish asks.
Enter (a+)+ as a regex → error shown, rule not saved; same for .*.*.*.*x and a*a*a*a*a*b.
Enter ^kubectl\s+(delete|drain)\b → accepted, and kubectl delete pod web-1 asks.
Enter [a-z]+[a-m]+[a-c]+$ as a regex → rejected; x+y+z+ and git\s+push\s+.*--force → accepted.

cards.title: Protected rules can differ per project, and either scope can reset to defaults
cards.user_does: Picks a project in the scope selector of the Protected actions section, toggles or adds rules there, or clicks "Reset to defaults".
cards.user_sees: Rules for that project only; a rule turned off for all projects shows as locked off with a note; reset asks for confirmation first.
rules: Scope choices: all projects, or each registered project.
Effective rules for a project: built-ins minus globally disabled minus project-disabled, plus enabled global custom rules not disabled for the project, plus the project's own custom rules.
Invalid custom rules (empty pattern, unknown match type) are silently skipped.
Resetting all projects restores the built-ins and removes global custom rules but keeps per-project settings; resetting a project removes only that project's rules and its turned-off list.
Reset is a destructive confirm, built into the page.
A custom rule added for all projects can be deleted only in the all-projects scope; inside a project it can only be switched off there. A project's own custom rules can be deleted in that project.
acceptance: Turn the deploy rule off for project A only → Claude in project A deploys to production without a prompt; in project B it asks.
Reset all projects → custom global rules vanish, project A's override stays.

cards.title: Recent protected attempts list shows what was paused and how it ended
cards.user_does: Scrolls to the recent-attempts list in the Protected actions section, and may click "Clear".
cards.user_sees: Up to 50 recent paused commands, newest first, each with the time, the worktree, the (redacted) command and an outcome badge: waiting on you (amber), allowed once (green) or denied and not run (red); an empty state when there are none.
rules: A paused command starts as waiting; it becomes allowed when that same tool call finishes or fails, and denied when the turn stops, a new prompt is sent, the session ends, or a newer attempt arrives in the same pane.
Only the newest 50 are kept, in memory only; restarting the app clears the list.
Stored commands are capped at 2,000 characters and redacted.
The list updates live in every open window.
acceptance: Deny a paused force-push → the row turns to the denied badge; allow one → the allowed badge.
Trigger 55 attempts → 50 rows; click Clear → empty state.

cards.title: Secrets in paused commands are masked before they are stored or shown
cards.user_does: Views the recent attempts after Claude tried a command that contained a key or password.
cards.user_sees: The command with the secret masked; Stripe keys keep their prefix and last four characters so the user can tell which key it was.
rules: Stripe live/test secret and restricted keys and webhook secrets are masked to prefix plus four dots plus the last four characters.

The general redactor then masks labelled key=value secrets, known provider keys (Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI, Google, GitHub, AWS, Slack, JWTs, PEM blocks), env-file lines, credentials embedded in any URL scheme, space-separated token/password flags and attached short password flags.
Already-masked Stripe values survive the second pass unchanged.
The raw key never reaches the attempts list.
acceptance: A paused command containing a live Stripe key → the list shows the prefix, four dots and its last four characters only.
mysql -pPASS, a --token value, and a postgres URL with user:password → all masked.

cards.title: The installed Claude hook passes on only an ask or a neutral reply, and keeps the settings file private
cards.user_does: Runs Claude Code with Kolux hooks installed; Kolux is closed, crashed or reachable.
cards.user_sees: Claude keeps working normally when Kolux is unreachable or the event is not a tool call; Kolux can only ever make Claude ask, never silently allow or deny on its behalf.
rules: The managed hook script prints exactly one JSON object: the neutral empty reply, or the protected-action ask reply; any other listener output is replaced by the neutral reply (audit S5).
Missing Kolux environment, non-tool events and listener errors all yield the neutral reply.
Windows and POSIX variants of the script behave the same.
Rewriting the user's Claude settings file to install hooks keeps its owner-only permission mode (audit S7).

Whatever the listener does (unreachable, a server error even with a decision-shaped body, an HTML page, several lines, extra text after the object, or a reply that stalls past the time limit) the script prints the neutral reply, exits successfully and leaves no temporary reply files behind.
Printing nothing is never allowed: Claude treats empty output from a permission hook as a refusal.
acceptance: Make the listener return an allow decision → the script prints the neutral reply instead.
Start Claude with Kolux not running → no hook error, commands run normally.
Set the Claude settings file to owner-only, reinstall hooks → mode unchanged.
Point the hook at a listener that answers with a server error carrying an allow decision, or that stalls → the script prints the neutral reply and exits 0, on both Windows and POSIX.
cards.compat: Managed hook script stdout contract: one JSON object, either {} or a reply beginning with the PreToolUse ask prefix.

cards.title: Network-share paths are refused before any file access (UNC/NTLM leak checks)
cards.user_does: Clicks or hovers a link to a path on another machine in markdown preview or terminal output, or something asks Kolux to open, probe or grant such a path.
cards.user_sees: Nothing is opened or probed on the remote host; the link does not act. Local and WSL paths, and shares that hold the user's own worktree, keep working.
rules: Host paths include double-backslash and double-slash host shares, file URLs with a host, the long-path UNC form, device pipes, and any double-backslash path that climbs with .. (which can land on a share).
WSL roots and long-path local-drive forms count as local.
A share inside a registered worktree root stays allowed.

Refusal happens before any filesystem call, so no credentials leave the machine; this covers markdown internal links, OSC 8 terminal links (plain and file), terminal link hover probing, path-exists checks and external file grants.
External file grants are exact paths only: never a directory, never a filesystem root, never a UNC path (audit I2 and I5).
On POSIX a leading double slash is just a local path.
Markdown images whose source is a file or host path pass the same textual check before any file access.

Path checks in the app core treat a leading double slash on POSIX as local, while link clicks in the interface refuse such links on every platform (a known fail-safe difference the rebuild may unify).
acceptance: Ctrl-click a terminal link to //attacker/share/x.txt or file://attacker/share/a.txt → nothing opens and no connection to that host is attempted.
A long-path local-drive form that climbs into UNC onto a host → treated as a host path and refused.
A WSL path link → opens; a share path inside a registered repo → still probed.
Grant access to a folder → not treated as a grant for the files beneath it.
A folder inside a repo that is a symbolic link to the home folder → granting it never exposes files beneath it (for example the SSH key folder).

cards.title: Executable files are revealed in the folder, never launched, from a link click
cards.user_does: Uses the open-externally click on a file link that points at a script, installer or shortcut.
cards.user_sees: The file's folder opens with the file selected; the file itself does not run.
rules: About a hundred executable or script-like extensions count, including Office/web-query oddities such as .one, .iqy and .slk.
Alternate-data-stream suffixes, 8.3 short names and trailing dots or spaces cannot disguise the type; a POSIX file with the execute bit also counts.
Colons or tildes in ordinary POSIX file names are left alone (audit I3 fix).
A Windows short-name pattern also flags ordinary names that look like one (for example a text file named with a tilde and digit); such files are revealed rather than opened, which fails safe.
acceptance: Shift-click open on a .bat, .js, .exe or .lnk link → its folder is revealed, nothing runs.
A name ending in .exe:stream or .exe. → treated as executable.
A plain .txt link → opens normally.

cards.title: Agents start in a new worktree without a folder-trust question eating the first prompt
cards.user_does: Launches Claude, Codex, Cursor or Copilot in a fresh worktree with an initial prompt.
cards.user_sees: The agent starts straight into the task instead of stopping on its own trust-this-folder menu, which would swallow the pasted prompt.
rules: Kolux marks the folder trusted in each agent's own config before launch: Cursor's per-project trusted marker, Copilot's trusted folder list, Codex's project entry in the Kolux-owned Codex home, Claude's accepted-trust flag.
Writes are idempotent, keep every other key and project, and never duplicate entries.
A corrupt Copilot config is never overwritten.
Codex writes queue behind one another; a linked worktree trusts its main repository root, and crafted git metadata can never widen trust.
Claude keys always use forward slashes and the on-disk casing (a backslash key would be ignored); an already trusted folder resolves at once.
acceptance: Create a worktree and launch Claude with a prompt → no trust menu; the prompt is delivered.
Launch twice in the same folder → trust file unchanged the second time.
cards.compat: Agent config files written: Cursor per-project trust marker, Copilot config trusted folders, Codex config.toml project trust, Claude config project trust flag.

cards.title: A whole wave of Claude worktrees is trusted up front so none loses its prompt
cards.user_does: Starts several Claude agents at once, each in its own new worktree.
cards.user_sees: Every agent starts cleanly; none stops on a trust menu even though they launch together.
rules: Before spawning, Kolux trusts all planned worktree paths in one write, up to 12 names per wave.
Paths are planned exactly as worktree creation would compute them; invalid names fail the same way.
Requests with an unknown agent, a missing or unknown project, an empty or non-text name list, a plain-folder project or a remote project are rejected; non-Claude agents are a no-op.
Marks arriving within a short window (about a quarter second) are batched into a single config write, so one Claude process flushing its config cannot erase a sibling's trust.
It is best effort: a failure never blocks opening the worktrees.
acceptance: Launch 6 Claude agents in new worktrees at once → all 6 paths trusted in one write; all start without a trust menu.
Ask to pre-trust 13 names → rejected before any path is planned.

cards.title: Kolux asks before running a repo's shared kolux.yaml scripts
cards.user_does: Creates or removes a workspace, or launches one with a linked issue, in a repo whose committed kolux.yaml defines a script.
cards.user_sees: A dialog showing the script and asking whether to run it, or, if a previously approved script changed, whether to run the new version; a checkbox to always trust this repo's kolux.yaml; buttons "Don't run" and "Run hooks".
rules: Covers the shared setup script (on create), archive script (on remove), issue command (on launch with an issue) and VM recipe.
Approval is remembered per exact script content (by hash), or for the whole repo when always-trust is ticked; a changed script asks again.
The content hash uses the platform crypto and falls back to a deterministic hash when that is unavailable.
Local, non-shared overrides never ask.
Prompts queue one at a time; closing the dialog, or another dialog taking its place, counts as don't run; later prompts still work.
Removing or re-adding the repo forgets its trust.
acceptance: First workspace in a repo with a setup script → dialog shown; Don't run → script skipped.
Approve, then edit the script → next create asks again with the changed wording.
Another modal opens over the prompt → the script does not run, and the next prompt still appears.

cards.title: Stored secrets stay sealed by the OS keyring and never fall back to plain text
cards.user_does: Saves a proxy URL, a search session link, a Claude token or a Grok key in Kolux, including while the OS keyring is unavailable.
cards.user_sees: The value works after restart; if the keyring is down, Kolux reports the secret store problem instead of quietly saving plain text, and a value the user cleared stays cleared.
rules: Sealed slots: HTTP proxy URL, browser search-session link, Claude OAuth token, Grok API key.
During a keyring outage, previously saved ciphertext stays sealed (not exposed, not overwritten by later saves); explicit clears are honoured and do not come back when the keyring returns.
A slower, superseded write can never leave stale ciphertext behind.
An uninstalled secret store is surfaced as an error.
Secret fields are stripped from what the interface receives, so echoing settings back cannot erase them.
acceptance: Simulate a keyring outage, clear the Grok key, restore the keyring → the key stays cleared.
